title: Prompting Claude to stress-test your retrieval fusion arithmetic
text: Is third. That is the paraphrase gap measured. The revision, add dense retrieval real mini LM embeddings matching on meaning instead of words. Then fuse the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. Each candidate scores one over 60 plus its rank in every list it appears in summed. Ranks not scores because BM25 scores and cosine similarities are not on a comparable scale and report all three methods. Two pieces dense embed the query dotted against every passage embedding the vectors are normalized so that dot product is cosine similarity. Then fusion for every rank list a candidate appears in add one over 60 plus its rank. No weights, no tuning. That is the whole of reciprocal rank fusion and it is four lines long. The code query two at 0.6. The entity-centric weakness the chapter warns about did not show up at 12 passages. In the hybrid, the combination that is supposed to be the safe default, missed the paraphrase. Only plain dense went two for two. Here is why. On the paraphrase, the certification policy was sparse as number one and dense is number two. The right answer was dense as number one but sparse had it third. 1/61 + 1/62 beats 1/63 + 1/61 by a quarter of 1,000. Fusion did not reason about either list. It counted ranks and a confidently wrong ranking outvoted a correct one. So, sparse matches words and misses paraphrases. Dense matches meaning and here missed nothing. Hybrid usually helps and rarely hurts but usually is doing real work in that sentence and this run is one of the

Times it hurt. Two honest limits. 12 passages is too small to reproduce dense retrieval's known weakness on rare entities and one fusion loss is not a verdict on fusion. The chapter says the same thing. The honest summary is not the hybrid always wins. Let your turn paste this. Take my own document set and build all three retrievers, sparse, dense, and a fused hybrid. Then find me the queries where the hybrid is worse than its best single retriever and show me the rank arithmetic that made it lose. That second sentence is the one that earns its keep. Anything will report an average that makes fusion look good. Asking for the cases where it loses plus the arithmetic is what turns a default into a decision you can actually defend. Watch the right answer get outvoted. Vedant Chudaxsh Patel.
